abstract: Large infrastructure investments, such as railroads, in migrant-sending countries can reduce emigration costs and increase local development, with ambiguous effects on net emigration rates. This column examines how the construction of Mexico’s railroad network between 1880 and 1910 shaped migration to the US over more than a century. Railroad access raised emigration rates to the US about fourfold in the early 1900s, mainly by allowing people to migrate in steps, which relaxed credit constraints on international migration. A century later, long after railroads became obsolete, locations with historical access to railroads send fewer migrants, but they still send them to the same US destination. Railroads created self-reinforcing migration corridors that outlasted the infrastructure itself.
title: The short- and long-run effects of railroads on Mexico–US migration

abstract: Every institution in modern finance exists to manufacture and maintain trust across society. This column argues that artificial intelligence poses new threats to trust which can fundamentally endanger the financial system. Deepfakes and voice cloning make it hard to verify identity or trust visual and audio evidence. A further threat is asymmetric understanding, where AI agents act on decision rules and representations of the world that humans cannot interpret or audit. Policy must adapt to preserve accountability, build resilience against AI-enabled fraud, and protect institutional trust.
title: Trust beyond face-to-face contact: AI and the future of finance

abstract: Carbon inequality is an important dimension of climate justice because high-emission groups and climate-vulnerable groups are often not the same. If excessive emissions among high-income groups are not effectively reduced, mitigation burdens may shift toward lower-income groups whose emissions are largely tied to basic needs, leaving little room for further emission reductions. We examine whether gender equality reduces carbon inequality and through what mechanisms using a theoretical model and panel data for 153 countries from 2006 to 2019. We find that gender equality significantly mitigates carbon inequality by reducing income and wealth inequality, with stronger effects under greater democratization and lower corruption. The reduction in carbon inequality is driven mainly by lower emissions among high-emission groups, while the direct effects on low-emission groups are limited. These findings link gender equality to the structure of carbon emissions and highlight the roles of redistribution, social inclusion, and quality of governance in promoting climate justice.
title: Gender Equality and Carbon Inequality: Do Social Ideologies Matter?

abstract: We study how the demand for programming skills has impacted inequality. We create a new dataset with information on wages, employment, and software of Brazilian programmers, covering the period from the birth of information technology (IT) to the rise of artificial intelligence (AI). High-ability, high-wage, and highly educated individuals in key technology hubs are more likely to become programmers. Creating software is associated with higher wages and better career prospects for programmers, especially for those with specialized skills in AI and cybersecurity. These wage gains are concentrated among top programmers, increasing inequality within the profession. Therefore, increased demand for specialized skills in programming has contributed to wage inequality both within the programming field and between programmers and other occupations.
title: How demand for new skills affects wage inequality: The case of software programmers

abstract: We quantify how the gender wage gap emerges over the working life across 29 European countries using a life-cycle accounting approach. The framework separates the gender wage gap already present before first childbirth from a childbirth-related component and a post-childbirth-related component. The pre-childbirth component accounts for a large share of the gap in Central and Eastern as well as Southern European countries, while the childbirth-related component is by far the largest in Northern and Western European ones. We complement these findings using an alternative approach that relates the gender wage gap directly to worker, job and firm characteristics. The complementary proximate-characteristics approach shows that part-time work accounts for a substantial share of the gender wage gap in Northern and Western European countries, whereas a larger share remains unexplained by the observed worker, job and firm characteristics in Central and Eastern and Southern European countries. Although the results are descriptive rather than identifying causal mechanisms, they nonetheless suggest that further prioritising family policies and encouraging wider acceptance of flexible work schedules are particularly relevant in Northern and Western Europe. In Central and Eastern as well as Southern Europe, anti-discrimination policies and measures addressing gender stereotypes may also remain relevant.
title: Accounting for the gender wage gap in 29 European countries
